questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Keeping accents on capital letters
questions.learningObjective: apply the French rule that an accented capital keeps its accent
questions.stem: A school in France prints its notice in capitals and writes « ECOLE FERMEE AUJOURD'HUI ». A second school writes « ÉCOLE FERMÉE AUJOURD'HUI ». Which form is correct, and on what principle?

options.text: the unaccented form, since an accent is a mark of handwriting and cannot be drawn in capitals
options.misconception: imports the English convention of writing capital letters without accents

options.text: the accented form, since an accented capital is simply that same letter standing at the top of a line
either form, since French has no rule about accents on the letters a capital stands for
options.misconception: believes French leaves accents on small letters but strips them from capitals

options.text: the unaccented form, because the rule about accents applies only inside quotation marks
options.misconception: thinks the accent depends on the quotation marks rather than on the letter itself

questions.explanation: French counts é, è, ê, ù and ç as full letters of the alphabet, not as marks laid over other letters. A capital is therefore the same letter raised to the top of the line, and it keeps its accent exactly as a small letter does: É sounds like é, and Ç sounds like ç. The habit of stripping accents from capitals comes from English and from older French printing practice, and it leaves a French reader with a word that has been misspelled rather than merely under-accented. The same rule settles the sign on a door, the heading on a form and the first line of a title, since none of those is handwriting and none is a place where French forgives a missing mark.
questions.hint: Ask whether an accented letter in French is a letter in its own right or a mark added to another one.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The ligature oe written as one sign
questions.learningObjective: spell a Latin diphthong with the ligature the French alphabet provides
questions.stem: A bookshop window in Paris carries a painted notice that reads « Achat de livres d'occasion et de l'oeuvre de l'artiste ». Which single correction belongs on that shop window?

options.text: the word needs a circumflex on the first letter, since the vowel would otherwise be unreadable
options.misconception: supplies a circumflex where the real problem is a missing ligature

options.text: the two letters should be joined into the single ligature, so the word is « œuvre »
nothing is wrong, because French has never decided how this word is to be written
options.misconception: believes French has left the spelling of this word undecided

options.text: the two letters should be written apart, since the joined sign is a printing convention only
options.misconception: treats the ligature as a printer's habit rather than as a letter of the alphabet

questions.explanation: The ligature œ exists for one purpose: to write a Latin diphthong in a single character, which is why it appears in œuvre, cœur, sœur, œuf and in the family names ending in -cœur. Writing the two letters separately is a misspelling rather than a variant, and the 1990 spellings left the ligature alone, having worked on hyphens, accents, the diaeresis, the plurals of compound and borrowed words and the families that disagreed. The two letters also keep their vowels apart: « œuvre » is one syllable, and the plural « des œuvres » takes an s that the unjoined form hides. A shop window that writes « l'oeuvre » therefore commits two errors at once, one of spelling and one of number.
questions.hint: Ask how many letters the word needs and whether French has a single character for that job.

questions.topic: The circumflex and words that sound alike
questions.learningObjective: use the circumflex to mark a word whose vowel would otherwise change or disappear
questions.stem: A proofreader marks three of these four lines as wrongly accented, and is right to do so. Which of the four is written correctly?

options.text: « Je suis sur de mon choix », since sûr is the form that means certain
options.misconception: reads sur and sûr as one word whose accent is only a matter of politeness

options.text: « Posez le pot sure l'étagère », since sur before a noun takes a circumflex
options.misconception: believes every instance of sur needs a circumflex before a noun

options.text: « Je vous dois dix euros », since dois is the present tense of devoir
« Je vous du dix euros », since du is the past participle of devoir
options.misconception: confuses the article du with the past participle dû and so drops the mark

questions.explanation: « Je vous dois » is the present tense of devoir: I owe you. The past participle is dû, carrying a circumflex that also keeps it apart from du, the contraction of de and le, so a second line reading « je vous du » is wrong. The same job is done in sûr, certain, against sur, on, and in mûr, ripe, against mur, wall. The circumflex was never abolished: the 1990 spellings dropped it only where it had become decoration, and kept it wherever it marks a difference of sound, of length or of meaning. A reader who drops every circumflex loses dû against du on the page, and no listener can recover the difference afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask which pairs of French words would be written identically if the accent were removed.

questions.topic: The plural of nouns in -al
questions.learningObjective: apply the -aux plural to -al nouns and know the short list of exceptions
questions.stem: A stationer has typed four labels for a rail of paper: « des rideaus », « des balus », « des journaux » and « des animal ». Three of the four are forms a French reader rejects. Which one is right?

options.text: « des journaux », which is the form a French reader expects to see
« des balus », which applies the usual rule and misses the exception
options.misconception: applies the -aux rule without the exception that un bal takes a plain plural s

options.text: « des rideaus », which keeps the plural ending but loses the final s
options.misconception: keeps the plural ending -aus but forgets the s, so the word is still in the singular

options.text: « des animal », which drops the s that marks the plural of an -al noun
options.misconception: drops the s that marks the plural, treating -al as if it already closed the word

questions.explanation: A noun in -al normally takes -aux in the plural, and the s on the ending is not optional: un journal gives des journaux, un rideau des rideaux, un animal des animaux, un journal officiel des journaux officiels. A short, closed list of exceptions takes a plain s instead, and its members are mostly words for a party, a season and a rhythm: un bal gives des bals, un festival des festivals, un intervalle des intervalles. That is why three of the four labels fail, each in its own way. A learner who has only the rule writes des balus, and a learner who has only the exceptions writes des rideaus. The exception list is short enough to learn as words.
questions.hint: Ask which of the six nouns whose plural you were given belong to the small group that takes a plain s.

questions.topic: The plural of nouns in -eau
questions.learningObjective: choose between the -eaux and the -eaux-with-s plurals of -eau nouns
questions.stem: A costume workshop has written four labels for a rail. Three of them are forms a French reader accepts without hesitation, and one is not. Which one?

options.text: « des chapeau » on the rail of bonnets, because a plural in -eau takes no mark at all
options.misconception: assumes a plural in -eau needs no mark of any kind

options.text: « des rideaux » on the rail of curtains, because a plural in -eau must end in -eaux
options.misconception: assumes every -eau noun must end in -eaux in the plural

options.text: « des peaux » on the rail of hides, because -eau nouns form the plural with a bare s
« des chapeaux » on the rail of hats, because -eau nouns drop the e in the plural
options.misconception: believes the silent e of the ending is dropped in the plural

questions.explanation: Most nouns in -eau take an s in the plural: un chapeau gives des chapeaux, un rideau des rideaux, un bureau des bureaux, un couteau des couteaux. A short group keeps the silent e instead: une peau gives des peaux, une eau des eaux, un lieu des lieux, un château des châteaux. Both endings are standard French, so the real error is neither of them but a plural with no mark at all. The trap for a learner is that the two rules live in the same word family, and the sound does not tell you which one applies, since peau and chapeau are pronounced alike. A learner who has only learned the s rule produces peaux correctly and chapeau incorrectly, and the reverse is just as easy.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four labels is not a plural at all, rather than which ending is unusual.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: quatre-vingts before a noun and before a numeral
questions.learningObjective: place the plural mark on quatre-vingts by looking at the word that follows it
questions.stem: A bookseller's price list is read aloud to a customer. Which of these four written forms is the one a French reader expects?

options.text: « quatre-vingt-dix » carrying no s, and « quatre-vingts millions » dropping the mark
options.misconception: believes a following million counts as a numeral that removes the mark

options.text: « quatre-vingt livres » with a noun after it, and « quatre-vingts dix » before another numeral
options.misconception: keeps the s before another numeral and drops it before a noun, which reverses the test

options.text: « quatre-vingt-dix-neuf » carrying an s, because the last element of a number is a noun
options.misconception: treats the last element of a compound number as though it were a noun

options.text: « quatre-vingts livres » with a noun after it, and « quatre-vingt-dix » before another numeral

questions.explanation: The plural mark on vingt and cent follows one rule, and it turns on what follows the number. The mark is kept when the word multiplies a figure and is then followed by a noun: « quatre-vingts livres », « deux cents euros », « quatre-vingts millions ». It is dropped when another numeral completes the number, as in « quatre-vingt-dix » and « quatre-vingt-cinq », and also when mille follows, as in « quatre-vingt mille » and « deux cent mille ». Note the contrast inside that pair: millions is a common noun and takes the s, while mille is read as the noun a thousand and never varies. The 1990 spellings added hyphens throughout compound numerals, writing « deux-cents » and « cent-trois » where older usage wrote them in two words, and left the mark itself where it was.
questions.hint: Ask whether what follows the number is another numeral, the word mille, or a common noun such as livres.

questions.topic: The plural mark on cent in deux cents
questions.learningObjective: explain why the s appears in deux cents and not in deux cent cinq
questions.stem: A theatre ticket reads « deux cents places » while a rent notice reads « deux cent cinq euros par mois ». What decides the difference in those two written forms?

options.text: The s stands only when the figure is a multiple of a hundred, and deux cent cinq is not one
options.misconception: puts the s in whenever the figure is a multiple of a hundred, even when a numeral follows

options.text: The s stands only when the number is written out in letters and the figures are left bare
options.misconception: believes the written s on cent depends on whether words or figures are used

options.text: The s is optional throughout, and the 1990 spellings abolished it wherever a numeral follows
options.misconception: believes the 1990 spellings abolished the mark on cent altogether

options.text: The s belongs to the currency word and is dropped when the figure is followed by euros

What does keep it is a common noun that follows, so « deux cents millions d'années » and « deux cents milliers d'habitants » are correct. The 1990 spellings added hyphens throughout compound numerals and touched none of this, which is why the deciding question is still the one to ask: has another numeral closed the number, or has a noun come after it?

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: What the 1990 French spellings do and do not change
questions.learningObjective: state the scope and the limits of the 1990 French spelling recommendations
questions.stem: A publisher in 1993 reprints a novel first printed in 1962 and sets a textbook written that same year. Which spelling practice do the 1990 French spellings call for?

options.text: the old spellings in the reprint and the recommended spellings in the textbook
the old spellings in both, because a recommendation can never bind a later printing
options.misconception: believes a recommendation has no force on any printing made after it

options.text: the recommended spellings in the reprint, since the change reaches back to every earlier text
options.misconception: believes the 1990 spellings reach backwards and re-spell books already in print

options.text: the recommended spellings in both, because no part of the 1990 change was ever optional
options.misconception: believes the 1990 change was a single rule with no date limit and no discretion

questions.explanation: The 1990 French spellings are recommendations, not a law, and they carry a date limit of their own. They were published on 6 December 1990 in the administrative section of the Journal officiel, they were meant for documents produced from that point onward, and they do not reach into a facsimile of a 1962 text. Rewriting the spellings of an old work would falsify the artefact rather than improve it. For new production the recommended forms are the ones to set, which is why a 1994 textbook may use them beside a reprinted 1962 novel that does not. One further point governs any argument about them: where a word was changed, both the old and the new spellings stay valid, so no one who writes the traditional form has committed an error.
questions.hint: Ask what a facsimile of a 1962 book is: a new document or a copy of an old one.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The apostrophe between two small words
questions.learningObjective: recognise the two jobs the French apostrophe does in writing
questions.stem: A learner has typed « aujoud'hui » and « si il pleut » and asks for both to be corrected. Which account of the two mistakes is right?

options.text: « aujourd'hui » takes a hyphen, and « si il » is correct because the subject follows the verb
options.misconception: believes French joins its short words with a hyphen and never elides

options.text: both are correct as typed, since French never joins its short words with a mark
options.misconception: believes French has no mark at all for joining or shortening its small words

options.text: « aujourd'hui » is one word, and « s'il » elides the final vowel of « si » before « il »
both are wrong only in the typing, since the spoken form is the same either way
options.misconception: judges spelling only by how the two words sound when they are spoken aloud

questions.explanation: The French apostrophe does two jobs, and a learner needs both of them. It marks an elision, the swallowing of a final vowel before another word begins, which is why the language writes s'il, qu'il, j'ai, l'ami and n'est with the letter missing. It also joins the parts of a compound, which is why « aujourd'hui » is a single word built on « au », « jour » and « hui », and why « quelqu'un » closes the same way. The elision is not decoration: in « si il pleut » the pronoun cannot simply follow « si », so the correct form has to lose the vowel to be French at all. A learner who types « si il » has written a phrase the language does not build, whatever it sounds like when read aloud.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two errors is about the letters that are present and which is about the letters that are missing.

questions.topic: The narrow no-break space before a pause mark
questions.learningObjective: set the space that French typography requires before its two-part marks
questions.stem: A typesetter asks how the space before a semicolon should be set in a French book, and why the answer matters. What is the practice?

options.text: No space at all, because French follows the English rule and closes up before a semicolon
options.misconception: imports the English rule of closing up the space before a semicolon

options.text: The space is a narrow no-break space, so the mark can never be left alone at the end of a line
An ordinary space, and the risk of a line break there is left to the typesetter's judgement
options.misconception: treats a possible line break before a pause mark as a typesetter's preference

options.text: A full-width space, the same one French sets between a figure and its unit of measure
options.misconception: picks the right kind of space and then puts it in the wrong position

questions.explanation: French has a spacing rule English does not: a space belongs before a two-part mark, which means the semicolon, the colon, the question mark and the exclamation mark, and also inside the guillemets. In a printed book that space is narrow and unbreakable, so the mark travels to the next line with the word it belongs to instead of being orphaned at the end of a line. The same narrow space does separate a figure from its unit, as in « 12 h 30 », which is what makes the last option tempting and wrong: right space, wrong position. On a screen a plain space is understood and accepted, which is why the rule so often goes unnoticed online.
questions.hint: Ask what French does before a mark made of two characters, and what happens at the end of a line.

questions.topic: The French semicolon and the French colon
questions.learningObjective: tell the French semicolon and colon apart and set the French colon correctly
questions.stem: A style guide compares the two French marks that carry a pause. Which of the four pairings below does it actually teach?

options.misconception: swaps the two marks and treats the semicolon as the one that introduces

options.text: the colon introduces a full stop with a pause, and the semicolon is a comma inside a list
options.misconception: reads the colon as a full stop and the semicolon as a list separator

options.text: the two marks are interchangeable, so a writer may choose either wherever a pause is wanted
options.misconception: believes French leaves the choice between the two marks entirely to the writer

options.text: the semicolon binds two closely linked clauses, and the colon introduces what follows it

The colon announces what is coming: a definition, a list, a quotation, an explanation. One habit catches English speakers, and it is the one worth memorising: a French colon that introduces an example or an explanation is followed by a lower-case letter, so « trois exemple : le sel, le sucre » reads with a small e, and the same applies before « ! » and « ? ». A capital letter after a French colon signals a quotation or a proper name, so the lowercase is evidence, not an error.
questions.hint: Ask which mark announces what comes next, and ask what letter a French writer puts after it.

options.misconception: hears a grammatical label in a shop sign where an ordinary adjective is meant

options.text: both, because the shopkeeper is describing chairs that were never quite completed
options.misconception: reads the shop sign as a grammatical remark rather than a description of goods

options.text: the grammar book's, because that use names a tense rather than a quality of a thing
neither, since French reserves the word for a description of the weather
options.misconception: believes the word can only ever be used to describe the weather

A final vowel is dropped only after a cluster of consonants, which is why these two keep theirs
options.misconception: believes a final vowel survives whenever consonants cluster before it

options.text: Every final vowel is fully sounded, and the speaker is simply talking very quickly
options.misconception: believes every written letter must be sounded, however fast the speech is

options.text: A final vowel is dropped only in verse, where metre gives a poet leave to drop it
options.misconception: believes vowel-dropping is a licence granted to poets and to nobody else

The rule a learner can rely on is a negative one: a word-final vowel, including a silent h, is normally not sounded unless the speaker slows down, searches for the word, or contrasts it with a neighbour. Inside a phrase the effect is stronger, so « elle est belle » and « elle a raison » give up far more than the spelling suggests. The practical consequence is that the clear vowels of French sit in the middle of a phrase rather than at the ends of its words, and a learner who expects a sound after every written letter is waiting for one that is not coming.

questions.topic: The two nasal vowels of bon and banc
questions.learningObjective: recognise a French nasal vowel and say why two words with the same letters differ
questions.stem: Two words are written « bon » and « banc », with the same three letters after the b and nothing else different. How does a French speaker tell them apart?

options.misconception: believes the initial b is silent in one of the two words

options.text: by the vowel, which is nasal in one word and open in the other, and the n marks the difference
they do not differ at all, because an n before a consonant is never sounded in French
options.misconception: believes an n before a consonant is never sounded anywhere in French

options.text: by the meaning only, since French never uses the vowel itself to mark anything
options.misconception: believes identical spelling must always produce identical sound

That is why bon and banc sound nothing alike despite identical spelling, and why « pain » and « pent » do not rhyme. The n or m in these words is a sign of the nasalisation rather than a consonant of its own. A learner who has only seen the spelling will predict an English rounded vowel, which is a sound French does not use in that position at all.

questions.learningObjective: describe the place of articulation of the French r against the English one
questions.stem: A visitor asks why the letter r in « Paris » is not made the way the English r of Paris is made. What is the difference a teacher should describe?

A learner who substitutes the English r is still understood, but the substitution is marked at once and is among the last habits a learner drops.

options.misconception: believes careful speech and fast speech differ in the number of syllables

questions.topic: c'est a ... d'ici and the origin of a distance
questions.learningObjective: read a French distance formula and locate the origin of the measurement
questions.stem: A sign outside a village reads « C'est à dix kilomètres d'ici ». What does the phrase state, and where does the distance start?

options.text: A distance in two directions at once, because the phrase names both the town and the reader
options.misconception: believes the phrase measures from two separate points

options.text: A distance from the village itself, because the origin of a measurement is always the place named
options.misconception: believes the origin is always the place named in the sentence

options.text: A distance from the reader's present point, with d'ici naming the origin and the rest giving the figure
A distance in time rather than space, because d'ici is a phrase of time rather than place
options.misconception: believes d'ici marks a time rather than a place

questions.explanation: « C'est à dix kilomètres d'ici » means it is ten kilometres from here, and the shape is « c'est » plus « à » plus a figure plus « d'ici ». The particle « d'ici » supplies the origin, which is the here and now of whoever is reading the sign, and it is that phrase that makes the sentence a sign at all. When the origin has to be named, the pattern changes to « c'est à dix kilomètres de Lyon », where « de » introduces the place. Keeping « d'ici » in that second sentence gives the reader two origins and no measurement, and the same confusion returns with « à côté de » and « en face de », where a position and an origin are two separate things.
questions.hint: Ask which particle supplies the origin, and what replaces it when a place is named instead.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: jusqu'a against a partir de and pendant
questions.learningObjective: tell a French limit in time from a starting point and from a duration
questions.stem: A notice reads « Ouvert jusqu'à 18 heures » and a second reads « A partir de 9 heures ». What is the difference between them?

options.text: Jusqu'a marks a beginning and a partir de marks an end, which is the reverse of the English
options.misconception: reverses which of the two marks a beginning and which an end

options.text: Both mark the end of a period, and the two are simply two ways of saying the same thing
options.misconception: believes jusqu'a and a partir de mean the same thing

options.text: The first marks a limit that has been reached, and the second marks the point at which something begins
Both mark a beginning, and jusqu'a can only be used with a verb rather than a time
options.misconception: believes jusqu'a is incompatible with a time expression

questions.explanation: « Jusqu'à » answers the question until when, and it is used for a limit in time and for a limit in space alike: « jusqu'à 18 heures », « jusqu'à la gare », « jusqu'au bout ». « À partir de » answers the question from when, and it needs a starting point that is genuinely new: « à partir de 9 heures », « à partir du 1er janvier ». The pair that catches English speakers is « jusqu'à » against « pendant », since « pendant deux heures » is for a duration and « jusqu'à deux heures » is for a deadline. A sign that mixes the two will be read as saying something other than what was meant.
questions.hint: Ask whether the phrase answers until when or from when, and whether it names a duration.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: avoir plus an adjective
questions.learningObjective: use avoir with an adjective to name a state rather than possession
questions.stem: A speaker says « J'ai faim », « J'ai froid » and « Tu as raison », and a learner expects the verb to mean to own something. What is happening?

options.text: Avoir takes an adjective to name a state the subject is in, not a thing the subject owns
Avoir takes an adjective to name something the subject is carrying, so the verb still means to have
options.misconception: reads every avoir phrase as a claim of physical possession

options.text: The verb is a polite form of être, added to avoid stating plainly that the subject is hungry
options.misconception: believes avoir replaces être as a courtesy form

options.text: The verb should be followed by an article as well, and the learner has left that article out
options.misconception: believes an article is missing after avoir plus an adjective

questions.explanation: « Avoir » is far wider than possession. With an adjective it names a state of the subject: « j'ai faim », « j'ai soif », « j'ai froid », « j'ai chaud », « j'ai raison », « j'ai tort », « j'ai peur ». None of these says the subject owns anything, and a learner who translates them word for word produces something like I have hunger and I have cold, which is how the errors get in. The same verb also carries obligation and inclination: « j'ai besoin de », « j'ai envie de », « j'ai mal à la tête ». The test that separates the two uses is the adjective, since no French adjective in these phrases describes a thing that can be possessed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the adjective names a thing or a state, and whether anything is being owned.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: venir de for what has just happened
questions.learningObjective: mark a recent event with venir de and an uninflected infinitive
questions.stem: A colleague says « Je viens de voir le rapport » and a learner reads it as a statement about the future. What does the phrase mean?

options.text: The speaker has just seen the report, because venir plus de plus an infinitive marks a recent event
The speaker is about to see the report, because venir introduces an event that lies ahead
options.misconception: believes the infinitive after venir de points to the future

options.text: The speaker came from seeing the report, because de marks a place of origin
options.misconception: believes the de is the preposition of origin rather than part of a tense

options.text: The speaker will see the report, because an infinitive always points ahead of the verb
options.misconception: believes an infinitive can only be future by itself

questions.explanation: « Venir de » plus an infinitive marks an action that has just finished, and it is one of the commonest ways French shows recency: « je viens de manger », « il vient de partir », « nous venons d'arriver ». Neither venir nor the infinitive changes form, which is what lets the phrase work in a past narrative as well: « il venait de partir quand je suis arrivé » reports the same recency further back. A learner who reads the infinitive as a future will mistranslate the whole phrase, and a learner who has met only « je viens de Paris » will reach for a preposition where a tense belongs.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence places the event just before the moment of speaking or after it.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A verb of perception before a plain infinitive
questions.learningObjective: read the infinitive and the participle after a verb of perception
questions.stem: A report says « J'ai entendu tomber une tuile » and a colleague says « J'ai entendu l'arrivée de l'orage ». What is the difference?

options.text: The first perceives the action in progress with an infinitive, and the second reports it complete with a participle
The first reports a finished event with an infinitive, and the second one still in progress
options.misconception: reverses which construction reports an event in progress

options.text: Both use a past participle, and the only difference is which noun follows the verb
options.misconception: believes a verb of perception cannot take a plain infinitive

options.text: The first takes no complement at all, and the infinitive belongs to the sentence that follows it
options.misconception: believes the infinitive belongs to a following clause rather than to the verb

questions.explanation: « Entendre », « voir » and « sentir » take a plain infinitive when the action is perceived while it happens: « j'ai entendu tomber une tuile », « je le vois arriver », « j'ai senti la porte s'ouvrir ». The infinitive is uninflected, and the perception sits in the first verb, so the sentence says the event was under way. When the event is complete, a past participle arrives instead, as in « j'ai entendu l'arrivée de l'orage ». Both are standard French and the difference is one of aspect, which is why a learner who reaches only for the participle will report a finished event when the speaker described one in progress.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reported event had ended when the speaker perceived it, or was still happening.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The gender of a profession noun
questions.learningObjective: recognise that many French profession nouns carry no gender in writing
questions.stem: A notice reads « Docteur Dupont » and a second reads « Docteur Dupond est arrivée », and a reader checks both. What does the ending tell us?

options.text: Both name men, and the ending in the second belongs to the verb rather than to the title
options.misconception: attributes the ending to the verb instead of to the noun

options.text: The first names a woman, because a bare title is the form used for women on a notice
options.misconception: believes a bare title is specifically the feminine form

options.text: The second is a mistake, since a profession noun carries no gender in ordinary French
options.misconception: believes no French profession noun can show gender at all

options.text: The first names a person without naming a gender, and the second shows through its ending that a woman arrived

questions.explanation: A great many French profession nouns are written identically for men and women, so a bare « Docteur » or « Architecte » says nothing about which one is meant, and a notice that needs to know writes « Docteur Dupond » for a man and, where the form exists and is accepted, « Docteure Dupond » for a woman. When no such form exists, the ending on the rest of the sentence carries the gender, which is why « est arrivée » settles a question the bare title leaves open. A learner who reads « Docteur X » as a man, or who hears « un ingénieur » as necessarily male, is applying an English pattern to a system that does not use one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the written form alone says anything about a man or a woman, and what else in the sentence might.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: avoir l'air de against a plain statement of fact
questions.learningObjective: read avoir l'air de as a report of appearance rather than of fact
questions.stem: A friend says « Il a l'air fatigué » and another says « Elle a l'air d'avoir mal dormi ». What is the grammar and the point of the phrase?

options.text: It takes only a noun, so « fatigué » must be read as a noun rather than as an adjective
options.misconception: believes only a noun can follow avoir l'air de

options.text: It takes an adjective or an infinitive and reports an appearance rather than a fact about the person
It is a literary variant of être, and the two are interchangeable in every context
options.misconception: believes avoir l'air de can replace être in any sentence

options.text: It belongs to writing only, since a speaker would say « il semble fatigué » in conversation
options.misconception: believes the phrase is excluded from ordinary conversation

questions.explanation: « Avoir l'air de » reports how somebody looks rather than what is true of them: « il a l'air fatigué », « elle a l'air d'avoir mal dormi », « ça a l'air difficile ». It takes a bare adjective on its own and an infinitive after « de », which is what the second sentence shows. The phrase is a little more formal than « il semble » or « on dirait », both of which do the same work in speech, so a learner who meets it in a report should not conclude that speakers avoid the plainer verbs. What the phrase never does is state a fact about the interior, and that is precisely why a speaker chooses it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence commits to how somebody looks or to what is actually the case.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: s'en aller and a pronoun for a whole phrase
questions.learningObjective: recognise a pronoun that stands for a whole prepositional phrase
questions.stem: A friend says « Ça ne s'en va pas » and a reader asks what the pronoun covers. What is it standing for?

options.text: A single noun named in an earlier sentence, and nothing more than that noun
options.misconception: believes the pronoun can only stand for one word

options.text: A whole prepositional phrase, so the speaker avoids repeating where the thing is or is going
A courtesy pronoun added whenever a speaker is being formal with the listener
options.misconception: believes the pronoun is added out of politeness

options.text: The subject of the sentence, which it takes the gender and number of
options.misconception: believes the pronoun agrees with the subject in gender

questions.explanation: « S'en », « y » and « en » can all stand for a whole prepositional phrase rather than for a single noun, and that is what makes « ça ne s'en va pas » possible: the phrase is something like « de la maison » or « vers la gare », and the pronoun carries the whole of it. The same move appears in « s'en tenir », « s'en rendre compte » and « n'en voulez pas », where an idea rather than an object is being withdrawn. The trap for a learner is that the pronoun looks as though it refers back to one word, so « ça ne s'en va pas » is heard as a thing going away by itself, when both the thing and the direction were supplied earlier.
questions.hint: Ask what prepositional phrase the pronoun is standing in for, and whether it names a word or a whole expression.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: ce introducing a whole clause
questions.learningObjective: use ce in front of a clause to treat the clause as a single thing
questions.stem: A speaker says « Je sais ce que vous voulez » and « Montrez-moi comment vous faites ». What is « ce » doing in these two sentences?

options.text: It introduces the whole following clause as one thing, and the word after it supplies the question
It stands for a named person, and the clause gives that person's history
options.misconception: believes ce in front of a clause must be a person

options.text: It introduces a list of words, and the clause names them one after another
options.misconception: believes ce introduces a list rather than a clause

options.text: It is the subject of the main verb, and the clause explains that subject
options.misconception: believes ce is the grammatical subject of the main verb

questions.explanation: « Ce » can stand in front of a whole clause and treat it as a single thing. It is followed by « que » for a statement, « qui » for a person, and « comment », « pourquoi », « où » or « quand » for the other question words: « je sais ce que vous voulez », « voilà qui vient d'arriver », « regardez comment il fait ». In each case the word after « ce » is not a relative pronoun, because nothing has been named for it to refer back to. This is the French answer to a question English asks with a bare that, and a learner who tries to put « ça » in the same slot finds that « ça » cannot be relativised at all.
questions.hint: Ask what question the word after « ce » is answering, and what « ce » is treating as a single thing.
